papers.full_text: Reproduction numbers of Andes virus vary according to social setting Dear Editor, Andes virus (ANDV) is a South American orthohantavirus responsible for hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, mainly in Chile and Argentina. While hantaviruses typically spread from rodent reservoirs (i.e., the long-tailed pygmy rice rat), ANDV can cause human-to-human transmission. An outbreak of ANDV on a cruise ship departing from Argentina on 1 April 2026 highlighted the urgent need to understand the transmission dynamics. Although the overall transmission potential of ANDV is considered to be limited with the basic reproduction number (R0) at 0.24, secondary transmission is highly variable, sometimes involving superspreading events (SSEs). Identifying factors that drive heterogeneous transmission is crucial for efficient and targeted control of the outbreak. Here we aimed to estimate the reproduction numbers by social setting. We systematically collected dataset of documented human-to-human transmission of ANDV. We reviewed eight published studies and one official report of the World Health Organization from 1993 to 2026, including three reports from Chile, five from Argentina, and one from a cruise ship in 2026. From the transmission trees reported in the reviewed studies, we extracted the number of secondary cases generated by single primary case, and hereafter the distribution is referred to as the offspring distribution, stratified by social setting. We assumed that the number of secondary cases generated by a primary case in setting s (i.e., in household, hospital, or others) followed a negative binomial distribution with mean and dispersion parameter k assumed as common across setting. The probability of observing secondary cases is described by the offspring distribution . The likelihood was constructed from two components: (i) the zero-truncated negative binomial distribution among primary cases that generated at least one secondary case, which was normalized by , where is the probability of zero secondary case in a setting s, and (ii) a Poisson distribution for cases that generated no secondary case. Within each setting s, the ratio of primary cases without any secondary case to other primary cases that produced at least one secondary case is . Multiplying the ratio to ns, the number of cases generating one or more secondary cases, we obtained the expected number of cases without any secondary case. Summing up the expected counts of zero transmission over social settings s yielded the total number of zero events λ, written as . The observed number of cases that generate no secondary case, , was assumed to follow a Poisson distribution with mean λ. The total likelihood function was described by: Using equation (1), we jointly estimated Rs and k employing a maximum likelihood method with 95% confidence intervals (CI) computed by parametric bootstrapping. A total of 462 human cases were reported, and we excluded 17 cases that did not allow us to identify transmission tree in each cluster. Consequently, 445 cases were included in the analysis. Of the 445 cases, 55 cases (10.1%) had at least one secondary case. Of these, 41 cases caused secondary transmission in households, 6 cases in hospital (nosocomial transmission), and 7 in other settings including 2 during car trip, and one each for a bus trip, a workplace, a party, a wake (funeral), and on the cruise ship. The distributions of the number of secondary cases produced by single primary case for Andes virus, 1993-2026, by social setting Each panel shows the offspring distribution that was attributed to a specific social setting: panel A for households, panel B for hospitals, and panel C for other settings. Note that the vertical axis scale is different by panel. Blue bar shows the observed number of cases that produced specified number of secondary cases, and gray bar shows the model-predicted number of primary cases that did not produce any secondary case. The red line and point show the predicted counts derived from the fitted model. The reproduction number Rs for each setting s were estimated at 0.13 (95% CI: 0.09, 0.35) in households, 0.33 (95% CI: 0.01, 1.27) in hospitals, and 2.17 (95% CI: 0.37, 6.90) in other settings, respectively. The dispersion parameter k was estimated at 0.29 (95% CI: 0.16, 3.45). Fig. 1 compares the observed and predicted offspring distribution by social setting. Reproduction numbers Rs in households and hospitals remained below the value of one, but the expected value of Rs in other settings was above one. Other settings included closed and crowded indoor spaces (e.g. party and cruise ships) with a large number of susceptibles. Our findings lead us to suspect that prolonged close contact in poorly ventilated and crowded environment could potentially elevate the risk of transmission. That is, SSEs might be partly determined by environmental and social conditions rather than virus or host characteristics. While the hypothesized explanation needs to be validated, our findings offer an important public health implication. Focused interventions on specific confined spaces could efficiently help avoid and contain ANDV outbreak. Hiroshi Nishiura: Conceptualization, Investigation, Methodology, Validation, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing. Declaration of competing interest The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. From the transmission trees reported in the reviewed studies, we extracted the number of secondary cases generated by single primary case, and hereafter the distribution is referred to as the offspring distribution, stratified by social setting. We assumed that the number of secondary cases generated by a primary case in setting s (i.e., in household, hospital, or others) followed a negative binomial distribution with mean and dispersion parameter k assumed as common across setting. The probability of observing secondary cases is described by the offspring distribution . The likelihood was constructed from two components: (i) the zero-truncated negative binomial distribution among primary cases that generated at least one secondary case, which was normalized by , where is the probability of zero secondary case in a setting s, and (ii) a Poisson distribution for cases that generated no secondary case. Within each setting s, the ratio of primary cases without any secondary case to other primary cases that produced at least one secondary case is . Multiplying the ratio to ns, the number of cases generating one or more secondary cases, we obtained the expected number of cases without any secondary case. Summing up the expected counts of zero transmission over social settings s yielded the total number of zero events λ, written as . The observed number of cases that generate no secondary case, , was assumed to follow a Poisson distribution with mean λ. The total likelihood function was described by: Using equation (1), we jointly estimated Rs and k employing a maximum likelihood method with 95% confidence intervals (CI) computed by parametric bootstrapping. A total of 462 human cases were reported, and we excluded 17 cases that did not allow us to identify transmission tree in each cluster. Consequently, 445 cases were included in the analysis. Of the 445 cases, 55 cases (10.1%) had at least one secondary case. Of these, 41 cases caused secondary transmission in households, 6 cases in hospital (nosocomial transmission), and 7 in other settings including 2 during car trip, and one each for a bus trip, a workplace, a party, a wake (funeral), and on the cruise ship. The distributions of the number of secondary cases produced by single primary case for Andes virus, 1993-2026, by social setting Each panel shows the offspring distribution that was attributed to a specific social setting: panel A for households, panel B for hospitals, and panel C for other settings. Note that the vertical axis scale is different by panel. Blue bar shows the observed number of cases that produced specified number of secondary cases, and gray bar shows the model-predicted number of primary cases that did not produce any secondary case. The red line and point show the predicted counts derived from the fitted model. The reproduction number Rs for each setting s were estimated at 0.13 (95% CI: 0.09, 0.35) in households, 0.33 (95% CI: 0.01, 1.27) in hospitals, and 2.17 (95% CI: 0.37, 6.90) in other settings, respectively. The dispersion parameter k was estimated at 0.29 (95% CI: 0.16, 3.45). Fig. 1 compares the observed and predicted offspring distribution by social setting. Reproduction numbers Rs in households and hospitals remained below the value of one, but the expected value of Rs in other settings was above one. Other settings included closed and crowded indoor spaces (e.g. party and cruise ships) with a large number of susceptibles. Our findings lead us to suspect that prolonged close contact in poorly ventilated and crowded environment could potentially elevate the risk of transmission. That is, SSEs might be partly determined by environmental and social conditions rather than virus or host characteristics. While the hypothesized explanation needs to be validated, our findings offer an important public health implication. Focused interventions on specific confined spaces could efficiently help avoid and contain ANDV outbreak. Methods: Researchers compiled 1993‑2026 human‑to‑human cases from eight studies and a WHO report, extracted secondary case counts by setting, and fitted a zero‑truncated negative‑binomial model via maximum‑likelihood. papers.title: Hanta on the Hondius - public health and bioethical perspectives of the recent Andes hantavirus cruise ship outbreak.

source_records.title: Hanta on the Hondius - public health and bioethical perspectives of the recent Andes hantavirus cruise ship outbreak.

papers.full_text: Hanta on the Hondius - public health and bioethical perspectives of the recent Andes hantavirus cruise ship outbreak Background The outbreak of Andes hantavirus (ANDV) infection associated with a polar expedition vessel has been linked to at least eight confirmed cases and three deaths as of May 9th 2026. Following evacuation of three ill passengers at Cape Verde, the vessel arrived in Tenerife on May 9th 2026 under an agreement between the World Health Organization (WHO) and Spanish authorities within the framework of the IHR (2005). This editorial examines the public-health, regulatory, ethical, and cruise-industry implications of the event and highlights preparedness gaps relevant to future ship-related outbreaks. Regulatory architecture for ship health inspections International maritime-health governance is intended to prevent disease spread while minimizing unnecessary disruption to travel and trade. Relevant instruments include the IHR (2005), particularly Articles 19-28; the WHO Handbook for Inspection of Ships; the EU SHIPSAN framework and European Manual for Hygiene Standards; SHIPSAN inspection schedules and information systems; and EU Regulation 2022/2371 on serious cross-border health threats. Previous cruise outbreaks, including the Diamond Princess and Grand Princess COVID-19 events, exposed persistent ambiguity in flag-, port-, and coastal-state responsibilities, uneven port-health capacity, and operational difficulties involving evacuation and repatriation. Maritime public-health implementation has historically been inconsistent. Only 39.6% of European authorities reported routine inspections on national voyages and 35.4% reported routine port-to-port communication. A Spanish review found 22% of Maritime Declaration of Health forms non-compliant and 39% incomplete. Although frameworks evolved through HEALTHY GATEWAYS, HEALTHY SAILING and SHIPSAN, the overall inspection footprint remains limited. Challenges in initial coordination and response during the recent 2026 hantavirus event The currently ongoing event highlights several challenges listed below that are associated with the nature and the evolution of such an event in a distant geographical location. Person-to-person transmission The person-to-person transmission of ANDV in a cruise ship raises issues of infection control and prevention that are extremely difficult to manage. Issues include the potential for super-spreading and transmission before symptom onset. Handling of potential exposure and follow-up of vulnerable individuals is particularly difficult, especially since passengers can dynamically embark and disembark, including in isolated ports, while the event is still evolving. The long incubation time of the virus also contributes to the difficulty. Diagnostic, critical-care, surge-capacity, and deceased-at-sea limitations Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) may require molecular diagnostic tools to diagnose quickly. Pathogen-specific protocols for shipboard viral haemorrhagic illness are absent and limited by the absence of point-of-care tests. Even if samples were sent to land, few clinical microbiology laboratories have rapid in-house diagnostics for New World hantaviruses. Projecting from comparable VHFs, this lack of therapeutic infrastructure could result in high mortality differences between high- and low-resource settings for comparable VHFs. Advanced life support and mechanical ventilation are unavailable on most expedition vessels, and ECMO support is only available in specific regional tertiary care centers. Surge capacity in terms of adequate health care personnel is especially important in an event occurring in a remote setting. Deceased-at-sea handling may present significant logistical and bioethical issues. Biosafety without high-level isolation infrastructure Standard viral hemorrhagic fever precautions require impermeable gowns, N95 respirators, face shields, double gloves, and negative-pressure rooms with 6-12 air changes per hour. Cruise ships generally lack such infrastructure, raising uncertainty about achievable onboard biosafety. Dynamic passenger populations and the repatriation gap A significant challenge is the dynamic, continuously turning-over, passenger population that characterizes modern expedition itineraries - driven in part by commercial yield optimization toward multi-port embarkation/disembarkation models. This produces cohorts that are geographically and temporally fragmented across past, current, and future travelers. In 100- to 200-person expedition vessels with shared dining, lecture spaces, zodiac embarkations, and excursion groupings, every passenger has had plausible repeated proximity to others on board, placing exposure on a non-quantifiable risk continuum rather than in binary contact/non-contact categories. To our knowledge, no harmonized, binding international protocol exists for repatriation, post-disembarkation surveillance, or onward-travel restrictions of passengers from a vessel implicated in a high-consequence outbreak. During the recent outbreak a repatriation protocol was issued by WHO. The IHR sets broad obligations; the ILO Maritime Labour Convention establishes detailed crew repatriation rights but does not address public-health-driven repatriation in outbreaks; SHIPSAN binds neither third-country flag, port, nor home states; and according to previous reports WHO cruise-ship outbreak guidance is situational and non-binding. The result is bilateral, ad hoc negotiations involving chartered evacuations, embassies, charter insurers, and differing national quarantine policies. Vector surveillance and ship-borne biosecurity Rodent surveillance and integrated pest management on ships are less standardized compared to food and water hygiene protocols. An older study of 21 passenger ferries found that while no rats or mice were detected during active surveillance, three ferries had had rodents in the past, and the study emphasized that integrated pest control programs should include continuing monitoring for pest species in different ship locations. The IHR 2005 implementation for maritime transport has focused primarily on hygiene standards, with ship sanitation certificates and inspections emphasizing food safety and water quality, while comprehensive vector and rodent surveillance protocols remain underdeveloped. On another note, the establishment of new invasive species of vectors in remote areas is an important public health issue. Rattus norvegicus (brown rat) is the primary reservoir host for Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV), which causes hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in humans and has been reported worldwide in Asia, Europe, the Americas, and Africa. Maritime traffic plays a critical role in SEOV dissemination. SEOV has been detected in wild rats in numerous port cities including New Orleans and Hainan Province, China. Studies in Africa demonstrate that seaports and imported rats facilitate Seoul virus circulation, with Africa exposed to SEOV introduction events through exponential growth in maritime trade. On the other hand, Antarctica faces significant biosecurity threats from ship-borne introductions of invasive species like marine organisms and terrestrial invertebrates. Ship traffic connects Antarctica directly to global ports, with vessels from South Atlantic and European ports being particularly important vectors. Antarctic maritime traffic directly connects fragile ecosystems to global ports, and biosecurity incursions remain a major environmental concern. Coastal-state port refusals: ships are not isolation facilities Regional refusals of the cruise ship where the incident occurs illustrates how a coastal-state political decision can override IHR cooperation expectations when no binding mechanism for compelled humanitarian disembarkation exists. This, in our view, is the single most consequential public-health policy question raised by this event. It threatens to embed in maritime preparedness a principle that the public-health and cruise-industry literature has spent the past decade dismantling: the assumption that an outbreak-affected vessel can be safely isolated at sea while the underlying epidemic plays out. Ships lack negative-pressure isolation rooms, dedicated airflow, and the operational capacity to separate infected from non-infected populations. Crew-passenger interaction for routine ship operations - food and supply delivery, sanitation, medical care - cannot be eliminated, and shared ventilation and shared common spaces continue to function as transmission routes throughout any onboard quarantine. The COVID-19 maritime experience offers one well-documented illustration of this point: aboard the Diamond Princess, a 14-day onboard quarantine of approximately 3700 passengers and crew did not arrest transmission, and mathematical modelling showed that no single intervention or combination - symptom screening, viral testing, point-of-care diagnostics, telemedicine consultation, reduced numbers, restricted port visits - eliminated transmission risk at sea. The response to the Grand Princess, by contrast, achieved better outcomes through rapid, structured disembarkation to land-based federal quarantine facilities under coordinated multi-agency support, establishing the now-accepted policy preference for shore-based isolation under appropriate IPC over prolonged shipboard confinement. The principle is general, not specific to a respiratory pandemic pathogen. Although ANDV is thought to transmit less efficiently than SARS-CoV-2, the underlying logic is the same: indefinite shipboard confinement of passengers and crew with limited critical-care capacity, on an expedition vessel where every person has had repeated proximity to others, is unlikely to arrest secondary transmission and could expose others on board to disproportionate harm. The proportionate, evidence-based response to a high-consequence maritime outbreak is structured disembarkation to land-based facilities under appropriate infection prevention and control. The lesson of earlier maritime events is the reason to receive the vessel under appropriate IPC supervision, not the reason to refuse it; we urge that this point is not lost in future outbreaks. Bioethical considerations The response to the current event additionally raises distinct bioethical questions. Public-health emergencies require deliberate balancing of population health, individual rights and autonomy, fair distribution of burdens and benefits, and duty of care to those serving in the response. The situation can be even more complex in cases of emerging infectious diseases as legal precedent is missing by definition; the law should treat the affected passengers more like victims rather than vectors. Decisions on quarantine, port-access denial, prolonged confinement, and disembarkation restrictions must satisfy the established principles of necessity, least-restrictive means, proportionality, and reciprocity but also autonomy. ANDV does not transmit with the efficiency of common respiratory viruses; evidence for human-to-human spread is contested when shared rodent exposure is properly controlled for. The port refusals must therefore be weighed against the proportionality of indefinitely confining 140-plus people on a vessel, against the IHR-derived duties of cooperation among State Parties, and against the empirical evidence that shipboard quarantine is itself counterproductive. The dispersion of several passengers from Saint Helena, with confirmed cases now in Switzerland and established contacts in the Netherlands and South Africa, generates obvious tensions between public-health benefit and the privacy and self-determination of travelers that should retain their anonymity. Proportional, purpose-limited data handling, transparent communication to affected persons, and clear, internationally agreed, data-retention policies are basic ethical requirements that should be embedded in maritime contact-tracing protocols rather than improvised under emergency conditions. Similarly, the disembarkation of a passenger to Tristan da Cunha, a passenger who is now considered a probable case, presents an additional concern, as the island is only accessible by sea and only has limited medical facilities. A risk assessment of future disembarkations to remote islands that are, however, part of expedition cruises should balance risk to passengers with risk to others, including to local geographically populations. HCPS can frequently and rapidly require advanced critical care, and the medical evacuation of one critically ill patient to South Africa illustrates that geography, nationality, and insurance - not pathophysiology - too often determine whether a passenger receives advanced interventions. Justice-based public-health ethics demands that maritime preparedness frameworks specify, prospectively, who has access to such care, who pays, and how scarce evacuation slots and advanced interventions capacity are allocated. Crew members and the ship's physician are not passengers but workers under the ILO Maritime Labour Convention; they cannot disembark voluntarily, may have limited PPE meeting VHF standards, and depend entirely on shipboard infrastructure for any post-exposure care, with measurable infection risk including documented nosocomial ANDV transmission. The principle of reciprocity should be explicit in maritime frameworks, encompassing paid sick leave, long-term sequelae monitoring, and family support if death occurs in service. The current event includes deaths onboard, yet existing VHF mortality guidance is designed for land-based settings; this creates a major gap in maritime preparedness, as infection-control requirements must be balanced with cultural, religious, and family expectations for dignified care of the deceased and the timely repatriation of remains across multiple countries. Public-facing communication should be transparent, proportionate, multilingual, and updated as evidence emerges. WHO has assessed the global public-health risk as low and ECDC the European risk as very low; over-dramatization can fuel stigma toward travelers, indigenous communities, and sea travel, and can be instrumentalized to justify disproportionate coastal-state measures. Hantavirus events have historically been accompanied by stigma toward rural and indigenous communities; engagement with affected communities in Patagonia, rather than communication merely about them, is the ethical baseline. The psychosocial burden on quarantined passengers, on bereaved families notified across borders, and on crew remaining aboard a vessel after deaths and evacuations is well documented for prior cruise-ship quarantine events and is expected to be substantial; the risk of moral harm to clinical staff on board cannot be ignored either and will need to be addressed in time. In the future multilingual psychosocial support may be an issue to discuss in similar events from the outset. The cruise vessel ecosystem and lessons for maritime outbreaks The event under discussion is properly understood within the cruise industry's transformation since the COVID-19 pandemic. Global ocean cruise passengers reached 31.7 million in 2024, exceeding the 2019 record of 29.7 million, and the orderbook of approximately 58 ships through 2030 is the largest construction pipeline in maritime history. Demand has shifted toward smaller vessels and remote destinations, with luxury and expedition cruising - particularly polar - growing faster than the mass-market segment. The International Maritime Organization Polar Code (in force from 2017) and International Association of Classification Societies Polar Class designations prescribe ice-related and environmental requirements but do not prescribe public-health architecture beyond minimum medical-facility provision. Such vessels are optimized for ice navigation, not for negative-pressure isolation, in-house molecular diagnostics, or surge medical capacity. Naturalist and wildlife-focused expedition cruises involve repeated close ecological exposure through landings, lectures, photography excursions, and wildlife observation. The suspected exposure linked to a pre-embarkation bird-watching excursion exemplifies risks associated with these activities. Pre-travel risk communication should therefore reflect actual ecological hazards rather than generic gastrointestinal or respiratory guidance. The clinical response is anchored, in the first hours and days, by the onboard medical team - often a single physician supported by one or two nurses or paramedics - expected to function simultaneously as primary-care physician, emergency physician, intensivist for early stabilization, occupational-health officer, and public-health officer. On expedition vessels, additional skills (advanced trauma, intubation, zodiac landings carrying medical equipment over uneven terrain, multilingual communication) and current BLS/ACLS/ATLS/PALS certification are typically required. The combination is rare; the cruise-ship physician at the time of an outbreak onset is alone, geographically isolated, and tasked with decisions that ashore would involve an entire IPC committee. The structural undersupply of physicians with this blend of expedition, emergency, and infectious-disease experience is itself a preparedness gap. Maritime infectious-disease surveillance has historically been dominated by acute gastroenteritis (predominantly norovirus, occasionally Salmonella, Shigella, or Campylobacter from food-water cross-contamination) and influenza-like illness. Norovirus protocols emphasizing voluntary cabin-based isolation, environmental disinfection, hand-hygiene reinforcement, and graded restrictions on self-service food operations are empirically validated for self-limiting enteric pathogens but do not translate to ANDV-associated HCPS, which has a high case-fatality rate, requires advanced critical…

full_text_sections.full_text: Hanta on the Hondius - public health and bioethical perspectives of the recent Andes hantavirus cruise ship outbreak Background The outbreak of Andes hantavirus (ANDV) infection associated with a polar expedition vessel has been linked to at least eight confirmed cases and three deaths as of May 9th 2026. Following evacuation of three ill passengers at Cape Verde, the vessel arrived in Tenerife on May 9th 2026 under an agreement between the World Health Organization (WHO) and Spanish authorities within the framework of the IHR (2005). This editorial examines the public-health, regulatory, ethical, and cruise-industry implications of the event and highlights preparedness gaps relevant to future ship-related outbreaks. Regulatory architecture for ship health inspections International maritime-health governance is intended to prevent disease spread while minimizing unnecessary disruption to travel and trade. Relevant instruments include the IHR (2005), particularly Articles 19-28; the WHO Handbook for Inspection of Ships; the EU SHIPSAN framework and European Manual for Hygiene Standards; SHIPSAN inspection schedules and information systems; and EU Regulation 2022/2371 on serious cross-border health threats. Previous cruise outbreaks, including the Diamond Princess and Grand Princess COVID-19 events, exposed persistent ambiguity in flag-, port-, and coastal-state responsibilities, uneven port-health capacity, and operational difficulties involving evacuation and repatriation. Maritime public-health implementation has historically been inconsistent. Only 39.6% of European authorities reported routine inspections on national voyages and 35.4% reported routine port-to-port communication. A Spanish review found 22% of Maritime Declaration of Health forms non-compliant and 39% incomplete. Although frameworks evolved through HEALTHY GATEWAYS, HEALTHY SAILING and SHIPSAN, the overall inspection footprint remains limited. Challenges in initial coordination and response during the recent 2026 hantavirus event The currently ongoing event highlights several challenges listed below that are associated with the nature and the evolution of such an event in a distant geographical location. Person-to-person transmission The person-to-person transmission of ANDV in a cruise ship raises issues of infection control and prevention that are extremely difficult to manage. Issues include the potential for super-spreading and transmission before symptom onset. Handling of potential exposure and follow-up of vulnerable individuals is particularly difficult, especially since passengers can dynamically embark and disembark, including in isolated ports, while the event is still evolving. The long incubation time of the virus also contributes to the difficulty. Diagnostic, critical-care, surge-capacity, and deceased-at-sea limitations Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) may require molecular diagnostic tools to diagnose quickly. Pathogen-specific protocols for shipboard viral haemorrhagic illness are absent and limited by the absence of point-of-care tests. Even if samples were sent to land, few clinical microbiology laboratories have rapid in-house diagnostics for New World hantaviruses. Projecting from comparable VHFs, this lack of therapeutic infrastructure could result in high mortality differences between high- and low-resource settings for comparable VHFs. Advanced life support and mechanical ventilation are unavailable on most expedition vessels, and ECMO support is only available in specific regional tertiary care centers. Surge capacity in terms of adequate health care personnel is especially important in an event occurring in a remote setting. Deceased-at-sea handling may present significant logistical and bioethical issues. Biosafety without high-level isolation infrastructure Standard viral hemorrhagic fever precautions require impermeable gowns, N95 respirators, face shields, double gloves, and negative-pressure rooms with 6-12 air changes per hour. Cruise ships generally lack such infrastructure, raising uncertainty about achievable onboard biosafety. Dynamic passenger populations and the repatriation gap A significant challenge is the dynamic, continuously turning-over, passenger population that characterizes modern expedition itineraries - driven in part by commercial yield optimization toward multi-port embarkation/disembarkation models. This produces cohorts that are geographically and temporally fragmented across past, current, and future travelers. In 100- to 200-person expedition vessels with shared dining, lecture spaces, zodiac embarkations, and excursion groupings, every passenger has had plausible repeated proximity to others on board, placing exposure on a non-quantifiable risk continuum rather than in binary contact/non-contact categories. To our knowledge, no harmonized, binding international protocol exists for repatriation, post-disembarkation surveillance, or onward-travel restrictions of passengers from a vessel implicated in a high-consequence outbreak. During the recent outbreak a repatriation protocol was issued by WHO. The IHR sets broad obligations; the ILO Maritime Labour Convention establishes detailed crew repatriation rights but does not address public-health-driven repatriation in outbreaks; SHIPSAN binds neither third-country flag, port, nor home states; and according to previous reports WHO cruise-ship outbreak guidance is situational and non-binding. The result is bilateral, ad hoc negotiations involving chartered evacuations, embassies, charter insurers, and differing national quarantine policies. Vector surveillance and ship-borne biosecurity Rodent surveillance and integrated pest management on ships are less standardized compared to food and water hygiene protocols. An older study of 21 passenger ferries found that while no rats or mice were detected during active surveillance, three ferries had had rodents in the past, and the study emphasized that integrated pest control programs should include continuing monitoring for pest species in different ship locations. The IHR 2005 implementation for maritime transport has focused primarily on hygiene standards, with ship sanitation certificates and inspections emphasizing food safety and water quality, while comprehensive vector and rodent surveillance protocols remain underdeveloped. On another note, the establishment of new invasive species of vectors in remote areas is an important public health issue. Rattus norvegicus (brown rat) is the primary reservoir host for Seoul orthohantavirus (SEOV), which causes hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) in humans and has been reported worldwide in Asia, Europe, the Americas, and Africa. Maritime traffic plays a critical role in SEOV dissemination. SEOV has been detected in wild rats in numerous port cities including New Orleans and Hainan Province, China. Studies in Africa demonstrate that seaports and imported rats facilitate Seoul virus circulation, with Africa exposed to SEOV introduction events through exponential growth in maritime trade. On the other hand, Antarctica faces significant biosecurity threats from ship-borne introductions of invasive species like marine organisms and terrestrial invertebrates. Ship traffic connects Antarctica directly to global ports, with vessels from South Atlantic and European ports being particularly important vectors. Antarctic maritime traffic directly connects fragile ecosystems to global ports, and biosecurity incursions remain a major environmental concern. Coastal-state port refusals: ships are not isolation facilities Regional refusals of the cruise ship where the incident occurs illustrates how a coastal-state political decision can override IHR cooperation expectations when no binding mechanism for compelled humanitarian disembarkation exists. This, in our view, is the single most consequential public-health policy question raised by this event. It threatens to embed in maritime p…

papers.full_text: Transmission potential of Andes virus from human to human Dear editor, An outbreak of Andes virus (ANDV), a type of hantavirus (a genus within the Hantaviridae family) known to cause hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, has been reported on a cruise ship that departed from Argentina in April 2026. While the natural reservoir is long-tailed pygmy rice rat which is unique to South America, only ANDV among hantaviruses has a capacity to involve a certain number of transmissions from human to human. Because the reservoir rat is very specific to the virus, importation of human cases in Europe or North America does not immediately imply the introduction of disease for an extended period of time including in animal species. While human-to-human transmission of ANDV is also subjectively regarded as infrequent (due to the absence of pandemic by now), the transmission potential from human to human is the key factor to judge the absence of continued local outbreak, and thus, it is vital to firmly understand the transmissibility. Here we aimed to estimate the basic reproduction number R0 of ANDV except for the still-developing ongoing outbreak on cruise ship. Cluster size distribution of documented human infections of Andes virus, 1993-2019. Table Country Year Ref Total cluster size (persons) 1 2 3 4 5 16 34 Argentina 1993-2005 31 8 0 1 0 0 0 Chile 1995-2012 80 4 5 0 0 0 0 Argentina 1996-7 0 0 0 0 0 1 0 Chile 1997-8 22 1 0 1 1 0 0 Chile 2001-5 62 12 2 0 0 0 0 Argentina 2002 18 1 1 2 0 0 0 Argentina 2009-14 82 3 0 0 0 0 0 Argentina 2018-9 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 Total 1993-2019 295 29 8 4 1 1 1 Ref, references. Total cluster size included primary case, and thus, the category of 1 represents the absence of secondary transmission. We systematically collected documented human-to-human transmission events of ANDV (Table 1). In total, there were eight published studies from 1993 to 2019, including three from Chile and five reported from Argentina. There were 339 introductions to human population, involving a total of 448 human cases. Of 339 primary cases, 44 (13.0%) experienced at least one secondary transmission. Of these, 29 had only one secondary case, while 8, 4 and 1 introductions, respectively, resulted in a total of 3, 4 and 5 cases in each cluster. Other than these, two big clusters with 16 and 34 cases in total were reported in 1996-7 and 2018-9, respectively. Using the total documented cluster size distribution, and employing a negative binomially distributed offspring distribution which is known to capture realistic skewed patterns of secondary transmission, R0 and dispersion parameter k of human-to-human ANDV transmission were estimated at 0.24 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.18, 0.34) and 0.14 (95% CI: 0.08, 0.25), respectively. As an alternative approach, it is known that the proportion of cases with environmental exposure is equal to 1- R0. In the observed data, out of 448 cases in total, there were 339 primary cases, and thus 75.7% of cases literally had an exposure to rodent or contaminated environment. Accordingly, R0 was estimated at 0.24 (95% CI: 0.20, 0.28). In both analyses, R0 was estimated at 0.24 and was sufficiently below the value of one. Because sporadic cases are less likely ascertained than large clusters, and thus, it is likely that cluster size of one (i.e. no secondary case) is perhaps underestimated in its frequency, we may have overestimated R0. Thus, the actual transmissibility may be even smaller than what is presented here. Accordingly, assuming that the virus characteristics have not substantially changed from that causing past outbreaks in Table 1, we can objectively conclude that it is very unlikely that the outbreak that started from the cruise ship may not continue with sustained human-to-human transmission. Apart from R0, it must be noted that the secondary transmission is over-dispersed (i.e. accompanied by a large variance) with k = 0.14. This implies that the heterogeneity is highly influential, sometimes allowing a cluster to involve more than 10 human cases. Optimal conditions that allow such super-spreading event must be clarified in a neat epidemiological and environmental investigations, examining whether a large-scale transmission can be attributed to characteristics of primary case, those of exposed susceptible individuals, virus characteristics or environmental settings. Identifying environmental conditions allowing transmission of aerosolized particles is a common scientific task shared with investigation of environmental exposure, including whether the large cluster on the cruise ship had something to do with environmental exposure with limited air exchange rate. CRediT authorship contribution statement Hiroshi Nishiura: Conceptualization, Formal analysis, Investigation, Methodology, Validation, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing. Yuri Amemiya: Data curation, Investigation, Methodology, Writing – original draft, Writing – review & editing. Declaration of competing interest The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. References Clusters of hantavirus infection, southern Argentina Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, Southern Chile, 1995–2012 Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak in Argentina: molecular evidence for person-to-person transmission of Andes virus An outbreak of Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, Chile, 1997 Prospective evaluation of household contacts of persons with hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome in Chile Person-to-person transmission of Andes virus Síndrome pulmonar por hantavirus en Buenos Aires, 2009–2014 "Super-spreaders" and person-to-person transmission of Andes virus in Argentina

analysis.background: An outbreak of Andes virus (ANDV) was reported on a cruise ship departing Argentina in April 2026, and ANDV is the only hantavirus known to transmit between humans, making its transmissibility critical to assess.
analysis.methods: The authors systematically compiled documented human‑to‑human transmission events from 1993‑2019 (eight studies, 339 introductions, 448 cases) and used the cluster size distribution (Table 1) to estimate transmission parameters via a negative‑binomial offspring model.
analysis.results: The basic reproduction number was estimated at R₀ = 0.24 (95% CI 0.18‑0.34) with a dispersion parameter k = 0.14 (95% CI 0.08‑0.25); an alternative calculation based on environmental exposure yielded R₀ = 0.24 (95% CI 0.20‑0.28). Of 339 primary cases, 44 (13.0 %) produced secondary cases, with most clusters containing only one secondary case.
analysis.contribution: These findings demonstrate that ANDV transmissibility is well below the epidemic threshold and is highly over‑dispersed, implying that sustained outbreaks are unlikely but super‑spreaders can occur; this informs surveillance and control strategies.
analysis.limitations: The authors note that cluster size 1 may be underestimated, potentially inflating R₀, and that the analysis relies on published case reports, which may miss sporadic cases; thus the true transmissibility may be even lower.

Of 339 primary cases, 44 (13.0 %) produced secondary cases, with most clusters containing only one secondary case. papers.title: "Hantavirus at sea: Why cruise ships must be ready for animal-borne disease.".

source_records.title: "Hantavirus at sea: Why cruise ships must be ready for animal-borne disease.".

papers.full_text: “Hantavirus at sea: Why cruise ships must be ready for animal-borne disease.” Dear Editor The suspected cluster of hantavirus infections on a cruise ship, widely reported in the media, should not be dismissed as a curiosity of maritime travel; it is a stark warning. This incident lays bare a structural flaw in global maritime health preparedness: cruise ships are engineered to manage predictable viral threats, such as norovirus and COVID-19, yet remain dangerously exposed to high-fatality, environmentally transmitted zoonoses sustained by rodent reservoirs. Treating this event as an outlier misses its real significance: it is an early stress test of a system unready for the next wave of rodent-borne disease at sea. Hantaviruses are among the most pervasive rodent-borne zoonoses worldwide, with an estimated 150,000–200,000 human infections per year. The case fatality rates for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and hantavirus pulmonary/cardiopulmonary syndromes can reach up to 50% in severe cases. Transmission is typically through the inhalation of aerosols contaminated with rodent urine, droppings, or saliva in enclosed or poorly ventilated spaces. Climate change, intensified rainfall, and flooding are increasing rodent population densities and expanding habitats, tightly coupling hantavirus risk to environmental and ecological disruptions. No widely effective antiviral treatment exists, vaccines are limited in availability and uncertain in effectiveness, and management depends largely on early recognition and intensive supportive care. In contrast, the evidence base guiding infectious disease prevention, mitigation, and management on passenger ships overwhelmingly concentrates on respiratory and gastrointestinal infections. A recent scoping review of 620 publications on passenger ships and ports found that about half concerned respiratory illnesses and 11.5% gastroenteritis, while vector-borne and other “non-routine” infections occupied only a marginal share; rodent-borne pathogens were essentially absent from this literature. Guidance, drills, and infrastructure have thus been optimized to repeat the response to COVID-19 and norovirus, not to anticipate rare but catastrophic rodent-associated threats. Port and seaport studies clarify the risks of this omission for cruise operations. Surveillance in African seaports has highlighted that imported rats can introduce and sustain the circulation of Seoul ortho hantavirus (SEOV), with strengthened rodent surveillance and rapid elimination in port areas explicitly recommended to prevent human outbreaks. In Hainan, China, 11.7% of rats trapped around major seaports were hantavirus-positive, and phylogenetic analysis suggested that the introduction and spread were facilitated by maritime trade and waterborne transport of infected rodents and cargo. The authors warned that convenient water transportation and high rodent abundance may accelerate the spread to other regions and even internationally, and explicitly argued that capturing and eliminating rodents on ships is essential to prevent hantavirus disease outbreaks. Therefore, the public health implications of a hantavirus signal at sea are profound. Cruise ships connect ecologically distinct regions and can act as amplifiers and disseminators of rodent-borne viruses, exposing passengers, crew, dock workers, and port communities. Because severe hantavirus infections require advanced critical care, an outbreak at sea risks overwhelming shipboard facilities and small-port hospitals. In an era of climate-driven rodent expansion, economic globalization, and intensifying maritime trade, the failure to integrate rodent-borne zoonoses into maritime preparedness is no longer defensible. This event should trigger immediate policy action by maritime authorities and the World Health Organization. First, rodent-borne zoonoses, including hantaviruses, must be explicitly embedded into the International Health Regulations implementation for ships and ports, including standard case definitions, outbreak investigation protocols, and requirements for environmental and rodent surveillance. Second, mandatory and auditable rodent management plans covering structural rodent-proofing, active monitoring, and rapid control should be enforced for cruise ships and high-traffic ports, particularly in tropical and monsoon climates that favor rodent proliferation. Third, clinical and laboratory preparedness must be upgraded through training to recognize hantavirus syndromes, pre-agreed medical evacuation pathways, and access to reference laboratories capable of hantavirus diagnostics. The message from “hantavirus at sea” is unambiguous: a maritime health system calibrated only to frequent, low-fatality outbreaks is unfit for an age of accelerating zoonotic emergence. Unless rodent-borne, environmentally transmitted pathogens are brought to the center of cruise and port preparedness, the next outbreak will not be a warning; it will be a failure of foresight on a global scale. Fatima Abdijabbar Ibrahim: Formal analysis, Funding acquisition. Anisa Hassan Elmi: Project administration, Resources, Software, Supervision. Yakub Burhan Abdullahi: Supervision. analysis.background: The letter highlights a reported cluster of hantavirus infections on a cruise ship, using it to illustrate a structural gap in maritime health preparedness for high‑fatality, rodent‑borne zoonoses.
analysis.methods: No original study design, sample collection, or analytical methods are reported; the article is a commentary that cites existing literature.
analysis.results: Hantaviruses cause an estimated 150,000–200,000 human infections annually with case‑fatality rates up to 50% for severe disease; a scoping review of 620 ship‑related publications found ~50% on respiratory illnesses and 11.5% on gastroenteritis, with rodent‑borne pathogens essentially absent; surveillance in African seaports identified Seoul ortho‑hantavirus in imported rats; in Hainan, China, 11.7% of rats trapped near major seaports were hantavirus‑positive, suggesting maritime trade facilitates spread.
analysis.contribution: The piece draws attention to the omission of rodent‑borne zoonoses from cruise‑ship health protocols and urges integration of hantavirus surveillance, rodent‑control measures, and clinical preparedness into International Health Regulations and maritime policy.
analysis.limitations: As a letter, it provides no primary data, relies on secondary sources, and its conclusions are speculative rather than empirically demonstrated.

analysis.summary_en: Background: A reported hantavirus cluster on a cruise ship exposes a gap in maritime preparedness for rodent‑borne zoonoses. Methods: No original methods are presented; the article is a commentary citing existing studies. Results: Hantaviruses cause 150,000–200,000 infections yearly with up to 50% fatality in severe cases; ship literature focuses on respiratory and GI illnesses, neglecting rodent‑borne pathogens; African port surveillance found Seoul hantavirus in rats, and 11.7% of rats near Hainan ports were positive, indicating trade‑linked spread. Contribution: The letter urges inclusion of hantavirus surveillance, rodent control, and clinical readiness in maritime health regulations. Limitations: No primary data are provided; conclusions are based on secondary evidence and remain speculative.

papers.title_zh: "汉坦病毒 在海上:为何邮轮必须为动物源疾病做好准备。".

analysis_zh.background: 该信函强调了在一艘邮轮上报告的 汉坦病毒 感染聚集,并以此说明在针对高致死率、啮齿动物传播的动物源性疾病的海事健康准备方面存在结构性缺口。
analysis_zh.methods: 未报告任何原始研究设计、样本采集或分析方法;本文为评论性文章,引用了已有文献。
analysis_zh.results: 汉坦病毒es 每年导致约150,000–200,000例人类感染,严重病例的致死率最高可达50%;对620篇与船舶相关的文献进行范围审查发现约50%涉及呼吸系统疾病,11.5%涉及胃肠炎,啮齿动物传播的病原体基本缺失;在非洲海港的监测中发现进口鼠携带首尔正汉坦病毒汉坦病毒;在中国海南,靠近主要海港捕获的鼠类中有11.7%检测为汉坦病毒阳性,提示海上贸易促进了其传播。
analysis_zh.contribution: 该文指出邮轮健康协议中遗漏了啮齿动物传播的动物源性疾病,并呼吁将 汉坦病毒 监测、啮齿动物控制措施以及临床应急准备纳入《国际卫生条例》与海事政策。
analysis_zh.limitations: 作为一封信件,本文未提供原始数据,依赖二手资料,其结论属于推测性而非经实证验证。

papers.title: Global hantavirus outbreak and the lessons to be learnt for India: epidemiology, clinical manifestations, investigations, surveillance and way forward
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic pathogens of the family Hantaviridae that are present in rodent and insectivore reservoirs. They are transmitted primarily through inhalation of contaminated aerosols. Globally, it causes two major clinical syndromes: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), predominantly in Asia and Europe and Hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCS), primarily seen in the Americas. The 2026 multinational Andes virus Outbreak linked to the expedition cruise ship MV Hondius demonstrated the potential for rapid international dissemination of Hantavirus through global travel, resulting in multiple cases, deaths, and large-scale cross-border public health responses. The outbreak highlighted the importance of genomic surveillance, international collaboration, contact tracing, and preparedness for emerging zoonotic threats. India possesses ecological conditions favorable for hantavirus circulation and has documented evidence of hantavirus-related viruses. The apparent absence of major hantavirus outbreaks in India may reflect surveillance and diagnostic gaps rather than the true absence of disease. Strengthening one health surveillance, laboratory capacity, rodent monitoring, genomic sequencing, and clinician awareness is essential to enhance preparedness against emerging hantavirus threats.
papers.journal: International Journal of Community Medicine and Public Health

papers.title: The Changing Landscape of Hantavirus Infections: A Narrative Review of Epidemiology, Pathogenesis, and Countermeasures
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic pathogens of increasing global public health significance. Their epidemiological landscape is rapidly changing due to ecological disruption, climate variability, urbanisation, and evolving human–animal interfaces. This narrative review synthesises current knowledge on hantavirus virology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical management, and emerging countermeasures, with a focus on developments from the past 5 years. Traditionally classified into Old World viruses causing haemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) and New World viruses causing hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS), this dichotomy has become increasingly blurred, with overlapping renal and pulmonary manifestations now recognized. Among the most consequential recent advances is the consolidated evidence for person‐to‐person transmission of Andes virus, documented among household contacts and during the prodromal phase, with viral shedding in respiratory secretions. Endothelial dysfunction remains the pathological hallmark of severe disease, driven by VEGF sensitisation, Src kinase and RhoA pathway activation, pericyte infection, and dysregulated inflammatory responses including IL‐6 trans ‐signalling. Concurrently, environmental and ecological studies have linked climate change, rodent population dynamics, land‐use modification, and urbanisation to increased human disease risk across multiple continents. Diagnostic strategies continue to rely on serology and molecular testing, while management remains predominantly supportive, with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) improving survival in fulminant HCPS. Importantly, recent structural virology advances have enabled the development of broadly neutralising monoclonal antibodies targeting conserved quaternary epitopes, as well as next‐generation vaccine platforms including DNA, mRNA, and prefusion‐stabilised glycoprotein candidates. Hantaviruses represent a paradigmatic One Health challenge at the intersection of environmental change, viral evolution, and global interconnectedness. Despite major progress in understanding transmission dynamics and endothelial pathogenesis, critical gaps remain regarding determinants of person‐to‐person spread, long‐term post‐infection sequelae, and the absence of licenced broadly protective vaccines or specific antiviral therapies. Future preparedness will require integrated surveillance frameworks combining ecological monitoring, genomic epidemiology, and clinical readiness within coordinated international public health strategies.

papers.title: Rabies, Coronavirus, and Hantavirus Surveillance in Bats From the Atlantic Forest of Northeastern Argentina.
papers.abstract: Bats are increasingly recognized as reservoirs of numerous emerging and re-emerging zoonotic pathogens. However, little is known about the distribution of most hosts and viruses and the role of each bat species in transmission, particularly in South America. This study screened for orthohantavirus, rabies, and coronavirus infection, and characterized bat communities from Misiones Province, Argentina, during 2022-2025. At least 14 bat species were captured 1214 times. Blood samples were tested for orthohantavirus-specific antibodies by ELISA. Buccopharyngeal swabs were screened by two separate real-time RT-PCR assays: a pan-lyssavirus assay and a pan-coronavirus assay. Lyssavirus rabies RNA was detected in two individuals (Sturnira lilium and Artibeus lituratus), representing the first confirmed record in S. lilium in Argentina. Coronavirus RNA was detected in two Sturnira lilium, one Carollia perspicillata, and one Artibeus lituratus. Two of these samples, corresponding to C. perspicillata and A. lituratus, were successfully characterized as Alphacoronavirus. No antibodies against orthohantavirus were detected. These findings confirm high bat diversity and viral circulation in frugivorous bats, supporting integrated surveillance.
papers.journal: Tropical medicine & international health : TM & IH

analysis.background: Bats are increasingly recognized as reservoirs of numerous emerging and re‑emerging zoonotic pathogens, yet the distribution of most hosts and viruses and the role of each bat species in transmission, particularly in South America, remain poorly known.
analysis.methods: During 2022‑2025, bat communities in Misiones Province, Argentina were sampled, capturing at least 14 species on 1,214 occasions; blood samples were tested for orthohantavirus‑specific antibodies by ELISA and buccopharyngeal swabs were screened with pan‑lyssavirus and pan‑coronavirus real‑time RT‑PCR assays.
analysis.results: Lyssavirus rabies RNA was detected in two individuals (Sturnira lilium and Artibeus lituratus); coronavirus RNA was found in four bats (two S. lilium, one Carollia perspicillata, one A. lituratus), with two samples characterized as Alphacoronavirus; no orthohantavirus antibodies were detected.
analysis.contribution: These findings confirm high bat diversity and viral circulation in frugivorous bats, supporting the need for integrated surveillance of zoonotic viruses in the Atlantic Forest of northeastern Argentina.
analysis.limitations: Only the abstract is available, so detailed methodology, species‑specific sample sizes, and statistical analyses are not reported.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Bats are increasingly recognized as reservoirs of numerous emerging and re‑emerging zoonotic pathogens, yet host and virus distributions in South America are poorly known. Methods: From 2022‑2025, bats in Misiones Province, Argentina (14 species, 1,214 captures) were sampled; blood was tested for orthohantavirus antibodies by ELISA and swabs screened with pan‑lyssavirus and pan‑coronavirus RT‑PCR. Results: Rabies RNA was found in two bats (S. lilium, A. lituratus); coronavirus RNA in four bats (two S. lilium, C. perspicillata, A. lituratus), two characterized as Alphacoronavirus; no hantavirus antibodies detected. Contribution: The study documents high bat diversity and active viral circulation, underscoring integrated surveillance value. Limitations: Only the abstract is available, limiting detail on methods and analyses.

papers.title_zh: 阿根廷东北部大西洋森林蝙蝠的狂犬病、冠状病毒及汉坦病毒监测

analysis_zh.background: 蝙蝠日益被认定为众多新发和再发人畜共患病原的储存宿主,但大多数宿主和病毒的分布以及各蝙蝠物种在传播中的作用,尤其是在南美,仍然了解不足。
analysis_zh.methods: 2022‐2025 年期间,对阿根廷米西奥内斯省的蝙蝠群落进行采样,共捕获至少 14 种蝙蝠,累计 1,214 次;血液样本通过 ELISA 检测 正汉坦病毒 特异性抗体,口咽拭子使用全狂犬病毒和全冠状病毒实时 RT‐PCR 检测。
analysis_zh.results: 在两只蝙蝠(Sturnira lilium 和 Artibeus lituratus)中检测到狂犬病毒(Lyssavirus)狂犬病 RNA;在四只蝙蝠(两只 S. lilium、一只 Carollia perspicillata、一只 A. lituratus)中发现冠状病毒 RNA,其中两份样本被鉴定为α冠状病毒;未检测到 正汉坦病毒 抗体。
analysis_zh.contribution: 这些结果证实了果蝠中蝙蝠多样性和病毒循环的高度,支持在阿根廷东北部大西洋森林开展综合性人畜共患病毒监测的必要性。
analysis_zh.limitations: 仅提供摘要,未报告详细方法、物种特异的样本量及统计分析。
